strengths: Strong empirical results on MMEB (36 datasets) and the MMEB-V2 video subset, showing a training-free MLLM pipeline can outperform several trained retrieval models and even surpass some MMEB-supervised methods.

Introduces an interesting analysis of lexicalization pressure in the final MLP layer, with probing experiments across model scales and architectures, and a simple remedy that consistently improves embedding quality.
Proposes controlled generation prompts that improve semantic grounding and task alignment, supported by ablation showing incremental gains.
Identifies and analyzes an LLM framing effect in reranking (e.g., Yes/No vs. True/False vs. MCQ), with context-free bias experiments, and proposes a simple MCQ reframing that improves robustness.
The framework is model-agnostic and demonstrated across Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA families and sizes, with additional qualitative support for omni-modal retrieval and long-video understanding.
The paper is generally well-written and provides a reproducibility statement with runnable code in the supplemental material.
weaknesses: The main comparison is not fully controlled: FreeRet is a two-stage embed-then-rerank system, while many strong baselines (e.g., VLM2Vec, UniME, GME) are embedding-only. The reported gains may partly stem from the reranking stage rather than the training-free embedding, and the paper does not systematically compare against supervised embeddings paired with the same MLLM reranker.

Key reproducibility details are missing from the manuscript: the number of top-k candidates reranked, candidate pool sizes, exact prompt templates, how MCQ scores are computed (logits vs. generated text), whether prompts were tuned on the benchmark, and inference cost/latency measurements. These details are important for interpreting and reproducing the results.

Several broad claims are not fully substantiated: 'preserves generative abilities', 'unifies retrieval, reranking, and generation into end-to-end RAG', and 'supports arbitrary modality combinations' are demonstrated only qualitatively or trivially; no quantitative RAG/generation or audio-video retrieval evaluation is provided.

The ablation tables are confusing and partly inconsistent. For example, Table 3a labels are garbled (repeated 'hMLP'), and the baseline in Table 3b (42.42/45.53) differs from the hMLP baseline in Table 3a (45.34/47.97), making it difficult to attribute gains cleanly to layer removal versus prompt engineering.

The framing-effect mitigation is confounded: the MCQ options still contain 'Yes' and 'No', so the improvement may come from the multiple-choice format or added explanatory text rather than neutral labeling. Positional bias in the benchmark MCQ setup is not fully controlled.

The limitations discussion is relegated to a brief appendix section and omits prompt sensitivity, computational overhead measurements, and ethical/bias considerations. The paper would benefit from a fuller discussion in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and timely question (can off-the-shelf MLLMs be used as retrievers without training?) and offers a plug-and-play, conceptually clean framework.

The two concrete findings—(i) bypassing the final MLP before the LM head to avoid 'lexicalization pressure' and (ii) the framing effect / MCQ reranking—are simple, verifiable, and plausibly generalizable; the probing experiment in Fig. 2 gives a reasonable mechanistic justification for (i).

The empirical evaluation is broad: multiple MLLM families (Qwen2-VL/2.5-VL/Omni, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV), multiple scales, 36 MMEB datasets, MMEB-V2 video tasks, and LVBench, with ablations on MLP removal, prompt constraints, and label framing (Tab. 3).

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: the prompting, embedding extraction, and reranking procedures are described in text and code is claimed in the supplement; the limitations section is honest about the compute overhead.
weaknesses: Confounded central comparison. FreeRet is a two-stage (embedding + MLLM reranking) system, but the baselines in Tab. 1 (GME, MM-Embed, LamRA-Ret, UniME, E5-V, etc.) are single-stage embedding models. The ablation shows embedding-only FreeRet scores ~50.7/53.7 (Tab. 3a) versus ~60.3/70.7 with reranking, i.e., most of the headline gain comes from reranking, which is far more expensive at inference. The abstract's claim of 'substantially outperforming models trained on millions of pairs' is therefore not a like-for-like comparison and is not supported as stated.

The 'training-free' framing is overstated. The three prompt constraints (task alignment, semantic grounding, noise suppression) and the per-task MCQ templates are explicitly hand-designed and evidently tuned against MMEB-style tasks ('You are required to assess if <placeholder> is related to <placeholder>'). This injects benchmark-specific priors that a truly zero-shot retriever would not have; calling the method free of supervision is misleading.

Insufficient efficiency/scalability analysis. Efficiency is central to retrieval, yet no latency/throughput numbers are reported, and the 'favorable balance between precision and efficiency' (Sec. 4.3) is asserted without evidence. Point-wise MLLM reranking over even hundreds of candidates is prohibitive; the claim of scalability to 100M candidates (App. A.5) is not demonstrated and relies on coarse pre-filtering that is external to the method.

The framing-effect study is thin: it is based on a single dataset (ImageNet-1K subset of MMEB, App. A.4), and the generalization of the 'LLM framing effect' claim is not established across datasets, tasks, or model families. The dependence of the effect on model scale (Sec. 4.3) is also only hypothesized.

Several broader claims are asserted but not empirically supported: 'preserves generative/conversational/reasoning abilities' (no before/after measurements), 'unifies retrieval, reranking, and generation into end-to-end RAG' (no RAG experiment), and omni-modal retrieval (Fig. 6 shows only qualitative examples, no quantitative benchmark).

The theoretical appendix (Lemma 1) is essentially a restatement that cross-entropy gradients lie in span(W); it does not formally establish the 'lexicalization pressure' claim, so it adds little beyond the empirical probing.

The video results (Tab. 2) show training-free FreeRet beating trained baselines by ~20 points (e.g., 58.3 vs 39.3 on video classification). Such a large gap is surprising and would normally warrant scrutiny of the evaluation protocol (frame sampling, candidate pools, reranking usage) relative to the baselines; the paper offers no such analysis, so the numbers are hard to interpret or trust.

Presentation/quality issues: Table 3a row labels are garbled (hMLP/hNen/hMLP/hMLP), Fig. 5 is truncated with no numeric values, and Fig. 1's sub-captions are duplicated ('(a) ... (a) ...'), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread. There are also inconsistent layer-count statements for the 3B/7B variants.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: whether off-the-shelf MLLMs can serve as competitive retrievers without any post-hoc training. The proposed FreeRet framework is simple, model-agnostic, and immediately deployable across MLLM families and scales.

The three interventions are well motivated and supported by ablations: bypassing the final MLP to avoid lexicalization pressure (+5.33/+5.71 on Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B), adding controlled prompt constraints (+8.25/+8.15), and using MCQ-based reranking (best in Table 3c).

The empirical results are strong. On MMEB, FreeRet-7B reaches 70.7 average, matching the best supervised model UniME (70.7) and outperforming many methods trained on millions of pairs; FreeRet-32B reaches 73.3. On MMEB-V2 video tasks, FreeRet substantially outperforms all baselines, e.g., 58.3 vs 39.3 for video classification and 33.6 vs 29.0 for video retrieval.

The paper demonstrates generality across multiple MLLM families and sizes (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen2.5-Omni, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV) and provides additional evidence on long-video understanding (LVBench gains of +5.2 to +6.0).

The manuscript is generally clear, includes a reproducibility statement, and provides code in the supplemental material. The probing experiments and framing-effect analysis are intuitive and well presented.
weaknesses: The main comparison may be unfair: FreeRet is a two-stage system that uses MLLM-based reranking over top-k candidates, while many baselines in Table 1 are embedding-only. The reported gains could partly reflect additional inference-time compute and reranking rather than a better embedding alone. The paper should report embedding-only stage results separately and compare against baselines given the same reranking budget.

Potential benchmark contamination is not discussed. Off-the-shelf MLLMs are pretrained on massive web data, which may include MMEB/MMEB-V2 evaluation images, captions, or videos. This could inflate the apparent zero-shot performance and weaken the central claim that training-free retrieval is competitive. A contamination analysis or control is needed.

Several broader claims are not supported by quantitative evidence: 'preserves generative abilities', 'unifies retrieval, reranking, and generation into end-to-end RAG', and 'supports arbitrary modality combinations' are illustrated only qualitatively or not evaluated at all. These should be toned down or backed by experiments.

Important experimental details are missing or underspecified: the number of reranked candidates in the main results, exact prompt templates per task, score normalization, how Precision@1 is computed in the two-stage pipeline, and whether baseline methods were allowed reranking. This limits reproducibility and fairness assessment.

The framing-effect claim is presented selectively. The main text highlights an 8.4% MCQ gain over Yes/No on an ImageNet subset, but averaged over 36 MMEB datasets the gain is 1.92 points for 3B and 5.44 points for 7B in Table 3c. The context-free bias correlation is also based on only four label pairs.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A.2 is weak. Lemma 1 only states that the gradient lies in the span of the vocabulary vectors; it does not rigorously show that the final MLP learns to project onto the lexical subspace, so the corollary is more intuition than proof.

There are minor inconsistencies and presentation issues. The text claims that discarding additional layers 'fails to bring further benefits', but for 3B the h_{L-1}^{MLP} result (51.04) is higher than h_Attn (50.67). Figure 1 caption duplicates '(a)', and there are typos such as 'stear' and 'concent'.

Novelty is moderate: the components combine known ideas such as prompt-based embedding extraction, final-layer bypassing, MCQ framing, and the known framing effect from Zhao et al. (2021). The main contribution is the strong empirical demonstration rather than a fundamentally new method.

strengths: Training-free two-stage framework is practical and plug-and-play: it requires no parameter updates, no auxiliary models, and no external data, while supporting multiple MLLM families and scales.

The probing study of lexicalization pressure is a clear and useful contribution: it identifies the final MLP as the locus of lexicalization and shows across Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA that bypassing it improves embedding quality.
The controlled embedding-generation prompts are ablated systematically (semantic grounding, noise suppression, task alignment), with consistent gains on MMEB.

The LLM framing-effect analysis is interesting and well motivated: semantically equivalent labels (Yes/No, True/False, Right/Wrong) yield substantially different accuracy, and MCQ reranking mitigates the issue, supported by context-free logit analysis and benchmark results.

Evaluation is broad: MMEB (36 datasets), MMEB-V2 video tasks, cross-lingual generalization, Flickr30K/COCO, multiple backbones, efficiency analysis, long-video understanding, failure cases, and a code demo.

The full FreeRet pipeline achieves 70.7 average Precision@1 on MMEB with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, matching supervised UniME-V2 (69.6) and clearly outperforming trained two-stage baselines such as MM-Embed+10 and LamRA+10.
The paper is well written and organized, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges computational overhead and dependence on the base model's multimodal ability.
The efficiency analysis shows that unifying embedding and reranking in one model reduces memory and latency relative to prior two-stage retrievers.
weaknesses: The main comparison is confounded by reranking candidate budget: FreeRet+50 reranks top-50 candidates while key baselines use top-10 or top-5. The claim of matching MMEB-supervised methods relies on a larger candidate pool, so equal-budget comparisons are needed to isolate gains.

Embedding-only FreeRet (53.7 with Qwen2.5-VL-7B) is below strong supervised embeddings such as GME (56.0); the headline performance mainly comes from the reranking stage, not from the training-free embedding alone.

Task-specific prompt engineering may overfit benchmarks: the paper states MCQ content may be adjusted per task, but gives no prompt-search protocol, sensitivity analysis, or per-task prompt details, making the 'training-free' claim weaker than it appears.

Novelty is incremental: training-free LLM embeddings, prompt-based representation extraction, and final-layer bypassing have precedents; the framing-effect finding is interesting but does not by itself constitute a fundamentally new method.

The theoretical lemma is a simplified argument rather than a rigorous proof: the final MLP is not trained solely to project hidden states onto the LM-head span, and the corollary overstates what the gradient argument implies.

Several claims are not quantitatively supported: preservation of generative abilities is trivially argued from no fine-tuning but not measured; end-to-end RAG is asserted without experiments; omni-modal retrieval and arbitrary modality combinations are only qualitatively illustrated.

Reproducibility is incomplete: exact prompt templates, reranking score computation (SoftMax(p(A'))), candidate-pool construction, and task-specific MCQ option design are not fully specified; the demo is limited to image+text-to-image retrieval.

Table 1 contains apparent inconsistencies and unclear grouping, e.g. two MMRet entries with the same LLaVA-1.6-7B backbone but different training data (26.9M vs 26.2M) and large average gaps (64.1 vs 44.0), which undermines confidence in baseline comparisons.

The framing-effect analysis is largely limited to one ImageNet-1K subset and one benchmark; the explanation that larger models are more sensitive to framing is speculative and not tested systematically.
Main results report Precision@1 averages without significance tests or variance across datasets, making it difficult to assess whether margins over baselines are robust.

Long-video and RAG applications are only briefly evaluated; the LVBench setup lacks details on how FreeRet retrieves frames, how many frames are reranked, and whether gains hold across broader video benchmarks.

strengths: Targets an important and timely question: whether off-the-shelf MLLMs can be used for multimodal retrieval without fine-tuning, and proposes a simple two-stage embedding-plus-reranking framework.

The proposed modifications are parameter-free and easy to implement, and the paper evaluates them across several MLLM families and scales (Qwen2-VL/2.5-VL/Omni, InternVL3, LLaVA-OV) with ablations and additional analyses.

The full FreeRet pipeline reports strong Precision@1 on MMEB and video subsets, and the paper includes useful qualitative analyses such as lexicalization probing, framing-effect study, efficiency measurements, error cases, and long-video sampling.
The paper includes an honest limitations section and a code demo, and the training-free angle has practical appeal if the central claims hold.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not apples-to-apples. FreeRet+50 (70.7) is compared to UniME-V2+5 (69.6), MM-Embed+10 (54.9), LamRA+10 (55.0), etc. At matched top-10, FreeRet (67.8) does not match UniME-V2+5 (69.6). The abstract/intro claim that FreeRet 'substantially outperforms models trained on millions of pairs' and 'matches the best methods supervised directly on MMEB' is therefore not supported at equal candidate budgets.

The method relies on task-specific prompt engineering. The embedding prompts include explicit task priors, and the reranking MCQ 'may be adjusted to suit the needs of each task.' This is human task-specific supervision, not a fully plug-and-play zero-shot method. Full per-task prompts are not provided, which hurts reproducibility and makes the comparison with supervised methods less meaningful.

Embedding-only performance is far below top supervised embeddings (FreeRet-embed 53.7 vs. roughly 70 for top methods). The large gains come from reranking, but reranking top-50 adds about 2.97s/sample latency versus 0.08s for embedding. The paper does not report candidate recall@k for the embedding stage, so the two-stage ceiling and efficiency claims are unclear.

The framing-effect analysis is weak. It is tested on a single ImageNet-1K subset, and the MCQ improvement is confounded with richer option content ('fully matches' vs 'does not match'), not just neutral framing. The claimed correlation between context-free bias and downstream accuracy is not quantified across tasks.

The lexicalization-pressure conclusion is overstated. Removing the final MLP helps, but for Qwen2.5-VL-3B h_{L-1} is even better (51.04 vs. 50.67), so the final MLP is not cleanly the sole locus of degradation. The theoretical lemma is a standard observation about gradients lying in the vocabulary span, not a proof of the proposed mechanism.

Presentation and reproducibility have multiple issues: Table 1 grouping is unclear; LamRA is cited as Lin et al. (2024) in Table 1; Table 8 has duplicate 'FreeRetr20' rows with different numbers; Table 5 has a typo 'hLAnn'. Exact prompts, task-specific choices, and variance for main results are not fully reported.

Several broad claims are not evaluated: 'preserves generative abilities' is not measured; 'supports arbitrary modality combinations' is only qualitative (Fig. 6); 'unifies retrieval, reranking, and generation into end-to-end RAG' is not tested as RAG. The main comparison also confounds backbone choice (e.g., FreeRet with Qwen2.5-VL vs. supervised methods with LLaVA-OV), so gains may partly reflect the stronger backbone.
The limitations section does not acknowledge the prompt-engineering cost, unequal candidate budgets, or missing candidate recall.

strengths: Training-free and plug-and-play: FreeRet requires no parameter updates, auxiliary models, or external data, and it generalizes across Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA families and scales (2B-32B) as well as omni-modal backbones, making the approach practical and broadly applicable.

The three technical components are concrete and supported by probing and ablations: bypassing the final MLP is motivated by lexicalization-pressure probing (Fig. 2, Fig. 7, Table 3a, Table 5); controlled embedding prompts improve performance stepwise (Table 3b); and MCQ reranking mitigates the framing effect (Fig. 4, Table 3c).

Strong and broad empirical results: FreeRet+50 reaches 70.7 average Precision@1 on MMEB, matching in-domain supervised UniME-V2 (69.6) and clearly outperforming trained two-stage baselines at the same top-10 reranking budget (67.8 vs 54.9/55.0). On MMEB-V2 video tasks, FreeRet-embed-2B beats VLM2Vec-V2-2B by 8.4% on video classification and 2.9% on video retrieval, with additional gains from reranking.

The paper provides extensive supplementary evidence: cross-lingual evaluation, Flickr30K/COCO results, LVBench long-video experiments, model-family generalization, efficiency analysis, error analysis, and a limitations section. The impact statement and limitations discussion are appropriate; no major ethical concerns are apparent.

The presentation is clear and well organized, with informative figures and tables. The framing-effect analysis is an interesting diagnostic contribution that extends MLLM evaluation beyond conventional QA.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is not fully controlled: the headline 'matches methods supervised on MMEB' uses FreeRet+50 (70.7), while the strongest supervised baseline UniME-V2 is reported at top-5 (69.6); at top-10, FreeRet (67.8) is below UniME-V2. Baselines are mostly shown with top-5/10 reranking, whereas FreeRet's best number uses top-50. The candidate-pool size per MMEB task is not specified, so the actual reranking burden and the role of the embedding stage are unclear.

Prompt engineering and task adaptation raise overfitting/reproducibility concerns: the embedding prompts and MCQ content are manually designed and 'may be adjusted to suit the needs of each task.' Exact prompts for all 36 datasets are not provided in the manuscript, and there is no held-out prompt selection or sensitivity analysis across tasks. This makes it difficult to assess how much of the gain is from generic training-free retrieval versus benchmark-specific prompt tuning.

The MCQ framing-effect claim is confounded: the MCQ condition changes not only the label framing but also the option text (e.g., 'A. Yes, the candidate fully matches the query'), so the improvement may come partly from richer decision criteria rather than neutrality alone. The framing analysis is also limited to an ImageNet-1K subset and essentially one backbone, without error bars.

The theoretical analysis is informal and overclaims: Lemma C.1 shows that the cross-entropy gradient lies in the span of vocabulary vectors, but it does not prove that the final MLP learns the projection P_W(h) or that orthogonal semantic features are necessarily lost. The causal story is better supported by the ablation than by the theory.

Potential benchmark contamination is not discussed: MMEB includes widely used datasets (e.g., ImageNet, COCO, N24News) that may overlap with MLLM pretraining data. Since FreeRet uses off-the-shelf pretrained MLLMs, this could advantage the training-free setting and confound generalization claims, even if trained baselines also start from pretrained MLLMs.

No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for the main benchmark results; some ablations show small differences (e.g., 3B MCQ 60.31 vs True/False 60.06). Single-run averages over 36 datasets may hide variance.

Some presentation and reference errors need correction: reference entries swap years/venues for BLIP and LLaVA-OneVision, and there are typos ('concent', 'Cross-Linguual', 'FreeRetr20'). Claims about preserving generative abilities and unifying RAG are asserted rather than empirically evaluated.

Efficiency is a practical limitation: reranking top-50 on 7B costs 2.97s per sample and 23.59GB (Table 10), and embedding-only FreeRet is well below supervised embedding models (53.7 vs ~70 on MMEB), so the method's strong numbers depend heavily on expensive MLLM reranking.
